about: Exam cues for the mind map (docs/cheatsheet/mindmap.html), one per service in tag-vocabulary.json. cue = when the exam wants this service; traps = the mistakes questions are built on; twins = look-alike services (vocabulary names); sheet = cheat-sheet page#topic or null; icon = icons.js key shown on the node (null for none); icons = extra icons.js keys that mean this service in the architecture diagrams; diagrams = extra diagram ids; domain = exam domain (1-4) used when the tagged questions don't settle one. Rebuild with: node scripts/build-mindmap.js

IAM.cue: Who can do what in an account: users, groups, roles and policies. Roles give temporary credentials to services and other accounts.
traps: An explicit Deny anywhere beats every Allow.
Give EC2 and Lambda a role, never stored access keys.

IAM Identity Center.cue: Workforce single sign-on to many AWS accounts and business apps, with permission sets, often federated from an existing identity provider.
traps: It is for employees; app end users belong in Cognito.

Organizations.cue: Group accounts into OUs, set guardrails with SCPs, and pay one consolidated bill.
traps: SCPs only limit the maximum permissions; they never grant any.
SCPs do not apply to the management account.

Control Tower.cue: Set up and govern a multi-account landing zone quickly, with preventive and detective controls built on Organizations.
traps: Control Tower orchestrates Organizations, SCPs and Config; it does not replace them.

Resource Access Manager.cue: Share resources such as subnets, Transit Gateways and Resolver rules with other accounts instead of copying them.
traps: Sharing VPC subnets (VPC sharing) is not the same as VPC peering.

Cognito.cue: Sign-in for your app's end users. User pools issue tokens; identity pools swap them for temporary AWS credentials.
traps: Need to call AWS directly, e.g. upload to S3? That is an identity pool, not a user pool.

Directory Service.cue: Microsoft Active Directory on AWS: Managed Microsoft AD runs a real directory; AD Connector proxies to your on-premises AD.
traps: AD Connector stores nothing in AWS; it needs the on-premises AD to be reachable.

KMS.cue: Managed encryption keys for almost every service, with key policies, grants, rotation and CloudTrail auditing.
traps: Cross-account use of a customer managed key needs the key policy to allow it.
Keys are Regional unless they are multi-Region keys.

CloudHSM.cue: Single-tenant hardware security modules you control yourself, for FIPS 140 Level 3 or keys AWS must never be able to use.
traps: You manage the users and keys; AWS cannot recover them for you.

Secrets Manager.cue: Store database passwords and API keys, and rotate them automatically.
traps: Parameter Store is cheaper for config values, but has no built-in rotation.

Certificate Manager.cue: Free public TLS certificates that renew themselves, for ALB, CloudFront and API Gateway.
traps: CloudFront needs the certificate in us-east-1; a regional ALB or API needs one in its own Region.

WAF.cue: Layer 7 filtering on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway and AppSync: SQL injection, XSS, bad bots, IP and geo rules, rate limits.
traps: WAF cannot attach to an NLB.
Large network-level DDoS is Shield's job.

Shield.cue: DDoS protection. Standard is free and automatic; Advanced adds a 24/7 response team and cost protection for scaling during an attack.
traps: Everyone already has Shield Standard; pick Advanced only for the response team or cost protection.

Firewall Manager.cue: Apply WAF, Shield Advanced, security group and Network Firewall policies across every account in an organization.
traps: It needs Organizations; it manages rules, it does not filter traffic itself.

GuardDuty.cue: Threat detection from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs: compromised instances, crypto mining, unusual API calls.
traps: It detects; it does not block. Pair it with EventBridge and Lambda to respond.

Inspector.cue: Scans EC2 instances, container images in ECR and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and network exposure.
traps: Vulnerabilities (CVEs) are Inspector; active threats are GuardDuty.

Macie.cue: Finds sensitive data such as PII and credentials in S3 buckets using machine learning.
traps: Macie looks only at S3.

Detective.cue: Investigate the root cause of a finding with linked graphs of logs over time.
traps: GuardDuty raises the finding; Detective helps you investigate it.

Security Hub.cue: One place for security findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and more, plus checks against standards like CIS.
traps: It collects and scores findings; it does not detect threats on its own.

Verified Access.cue: Zero-trust access to internal web apps without a VPN, checking user identity and device posture on every request.
traps: Remote access to a whole network is Client VPN; per-app access without a VPN is Verified Access.

VPC.cue: Your private network: subnets and route tables, security groups (stateful) and network ACLs (stateless), NAT, endpoints and peering.
traps: A private subnet needs a NAT gateway in a public subnet to reach the internet.
Peering is not transitive.
Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

Transit Gateway.cue: A hub that connects many VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect, with route tables to control who talks to whom.
traps: Many VPCs fully meshed means too many peerings; use a Transit Gateway.

Direct Connect.cue: A private, dedicated link from your data center to AWS: consistent bandwidth and latency, lower transfer rates.
traps: It takes weeks to provision and is not encrypted by default; run a VPN over it if encryption is required.
For resilience use two connections at two locations, or a VPN backup.

VPN.cue: Encrypted tunnels over the internet. Site-to-Site connects networks in minutes; Client VPN connects individual users.
traps: Quick and cheap to set up, but bandwidth and latency vary with the internet.

Elastic Load Balancing.cue: Spread traffic over healthy targets in several AZs. ALB routes HTTP by path or host; NLB does TCP and UDP with static IPs; GWLB inserts appliances.
traps: Need a static IP or millions of requests a second? NLB, not ALB.
Path-based routing and WAF need an ALB.

Route 53.cue: DNS with routing policies (failover, latency, weighted, geolocation) and health checks; alias records point at AWS resources.
traps: Use an alias record, not a CNAME, at the zone apex.
DNS failover depends on TTLs and client caching.

CloudFront.cue: A CDN that caches content at edge locations, with origin access control for S3, signed URLs and edge functions.
traps: Lock an S3 origin with origin access control, not a public bucket.
Signed URLs or cookies for paid content; S3 presigned URLs are for direct S3 access.

Global Accelerator.cue: Two static anycast IPs that carry any TCP or UDP traffic over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy Region, with fast failover.
traps: It caches nothing. HTTP content is CloudFront; static IPs, non-HTTP or fast Regional failover is Global Accelerator.

Network Firewall.cue: A managed stateful firewall for VPC traffic, with intrusion prevention and domain filtering for outbound traffic.
traps: Filtering outbound traffic by domain name is Network Firewall, not security groups.

Local Zones & Wavelength.cue: Compute close to users: Local Zones extend a Region into a metro area; Wavelength sits inside 5G carrier networks.
traps: Single-digit millisecond latency in your own data center is Outposts instead.

EC2.cue: Virtual servers. The exam turns on instance families, purchase options (On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved, Spot), placement groups and storage.
traps: Spot can be interrupted with a two-minute warning; only use it for fault-tolerant work.
Instance store data is lost when the instance stops.

EC2 Auto Scaling.cue: Keep the right number of healthy instances across AZs, with target tracking, step, scheduled or predictive scaling.
traps: Target tracking is the default answer; scheduled scaling is for known peaks.
Scale queue workers on backlog per instance.

Lambda.cue: Run code on events with no servers, paying per request and duration, for jobs of up to 15 minutes.
traps: Over 15 minutes, or long-running? Use Fargate, ECS or Batch.
Reserved concurrency caps a function and protects downstream services.

ECS.cue: AWS's own container orchestrator, running tasks and services on EC2 or Fargate.
traps: Task role for the app's AWS calls; task execution role for pulling images and writing logs.

EKS.cue: Managed Kubernetes. Pick it when the team already uses Kubernetes or needs portability.
traps: No Kubernetes requirement? ECS is simpler.

Fargate.cue: Run containers for ECS or EKS without managing servers; you pay for each task's vCPU and memory.
traps: Least operational overhead for containers means Fargate, not ECS on EC2.

ECR.cue: A private container image registry with image scanning, replication and lifecycle policies.

Batch.cue: Queue and run large batch jobs on managed EC2, Spot or Fargate capacity, with no time limit.
traps: Long jobs that outgrow Lambda's 15 minutes fit Batch.

Elastic Beanstalk.cue: Upload your code and it provisions and manages the EC2, load balancer and scaling for you, with deployment policies.
traps: The developers want to deploy code without managing infrastructure: Beanstalk.

Outposts.cue: AWS racks in your own data center, for very low latency to local systems or data that must stay on premises.

S3.cue: Object storage with eleven nines of durability, storage classes, lifecycle rules, versioning, replication and Object Lock.
traps: Unknown access patterns: Intelligent-Tiering.
Retrieval in minutes or hours decides between the Glacier classes.
Replication needs versioning on both buckets.

EBS.cue: Block volumes for one EC2 instance in one AZ: gp3 for general use, io2 for high IOPS, st1 and sc1 for throughput.
traps: A volume lives in one AZ; move it with a snapshot.
Multi-Attach is io1/io2 only, in one AZ.

EFS.cue: Elastic NFS file storage for Linux, shared by many instances and containers across AZs.
traps: Windows file shares (SMB) are FSx for Windows File Server, not EFS.

FSx.cue: Managed third-party file systems: Windows File Server (SMB, AD), Lustre (HPC, links to S3), NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS.
traps: HPC or ML needing very fast storage tied to S3: FSx for Lustre.

Storage Gateway.cue: Give on-premises apps access to cloud storage: File Gateway (NFS/SMB to S3), Volume Gateway (iSCSI) and Tape Gateway.
traps: Ongoing hybrid access is Storage Gateway; a one-off move is DataSync or Snow Family.

Backup.cue: Central backup plans across services, with cross-Region and cross-account copies and Vault Lock for write-once backups.
traps: Backups nobody can delete, even root: Vault Lock in compliance mode.

RDS.cue: Managed relational databases. Multi-AZ for availability, read replicas for read scaling, RDS Proxy for connection pooling.
traps: A Multi-AZ instance standby takes no reads.
Read replicas are asynchronous.

Aurora.cue: MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible, with storage copied six ways over three AZs, up to 15 replicas, Global Database and Serverless.
traps: Cross-Region disaster recovery with an RPO of seconds: Aurora Global Database.

DynamoDB.cue: Serverless key-value database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, global tables, streams and TTL.
traps: Microsecond reads: add DAX, not ElastiCache.
Hot partitions come from poorly spread partition keys.

ElastiCache.cue: In-memory Redis/Valkey or Memcached for caching database results and storing sessions.
traps: Caching in front of DynamoDB without code changes: DAX instead.

Neptune.cue: Graph database for highly connected data: social networks, recommendations, fraud rings.

Timestream.cue: Time-series database for IoT readings and operational metrics.

SQS.cue: A queue between producers and consumers, so each side scales and fails on its own. FIFO gives ordering and exactly-once processing.
traps: One message to many consumers is SNS fan-out, not one queue.
Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue.

SNS.cue: Publish once and push to many subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS), with filter policies.
traps: SNS does not keep messages; put SQS behind it for durable fan-out.

EventBridge.cue: An event bus that routes AWS, SaaS and custom events to targets by rules, plus scheduling, archive and replay.
traps: Reacting to AWS service events or running a cron schedule usually means EventBridge.

Step Functions.cue: Orchestrate multi-step workflows with retries, branches, parallel steps and waits for human approval.
traps: Chaining Lambdas by hand with queues is the wrong answer when a visual, retrying workflow is asked for.

API Gateway.cue: A managed front door for REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, with authorizers, throttling, usage plans and caching.
traps: Usage plans and API keys meter clients; they are not authentication.

MQ.cue: Managed ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ for apps that already speak AMQP, MQTT, STOMP or JMS.
traps: Migrating an existing message broker without rewriting code: MQ, not SQS.

AppSync.cue: Managed GraphQL APIs with real-time subscriptions.

SES.cue: Send and receive email at scale, such as transactional and marketing mail.
traps: SNS email is for simple notifications; bulk or formatted email is SES.

DR strategies.cue: Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active-active trade cost against RPO and RTO.
traps: Pilot light keeps only the data live; warm standby also runs a scaled-down copy of the app.

Elastic Disaster Recovery.cue: Continuous block-level replication of servers to AWS, with recovery in minutes.
traps: Disaster recovery is DRS; a one-time lift and shift is Application Migration Service.

Application Recovery Controller.cue: Readiness checks and routing controls to fail traffic over between Regions or AZs in a controlled way.

Application Migration Service.cue: Lift-and-shift servers to EC2 with continuous replication and a short cutover.

DMS.cue: Migrate databases with little downtime, using ongoing change replication; Schema Conversion handles engine changes.
traps: Changing database engines needs schema conversion as well as DMS.

DataSync.cue: Online transfer of files over the network from NFS, SMB or HDFS to S3, EFS or FSx, with scheduling and verification.
traps: Not enough bandwidth to finish in time? Snow Family instead.

Transfer Family.cue: Managed SFTP, FTPS and FTP endpoints in front of S3 or EFS, so partners keep their file-transfer tools.

Snow Family.cue: Physical devices to move terabytes to petabytes offline when the network would take too long, with edge computing. AWS closed Snowball Edge to new customers in November 2025: new designs use DataSync online, AWS Data Transfer Terminal to ship data in person, or Outposts at the edge.
traps: Work out the transfer time: if the link would take weeks, ship a device.

Cost Explorer.cue: Charts and forecasts of past spend, plus Savings Plans and Reserved Instance recommendations.
traps: Alerts before you overspend are Budgets, not Cost Explorer.

Budgets.cue: Alert, or take actions, when cost, usage or commitment coverage crosses a threshold, including forecasts.

Cost Anomaly Detection.cue: Machine learning spots unusual spend without you setting thresholds, and alerts you.
traps: Fixed thresholds are Budgets; unexpected spikes with no threshold are Anomaly Detection.

Cost and Usage Reports.cue: The most detailed billing data, delivered to S3 for analysis with Athena or QuickSight.

Cost allocation tags.cue: Tags activated in billing so costs can be split by team, project or environment.
traps: Tags must be activated in the billing console before they show up in reports.

Compute Optimizer.cue: Right-sizing recommendations for EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS, Lambda and ECS on Fargate from usage history.

Data transfer pricing.cue: Inbound and same-AZ private traffic are free; cross-AZ, inter-Region, NAT processing and internet egress cost money.
traps: S3 or DynamoDB through a NAT gateway costs money; a gateway endpoint is free.

CloudWatch.cue: Metrics, logs and alarms. Memory and disk use need the CloudWatch agent.
traps: EC2 memory is not a default metric; install the agent.

CloudTrail.cue: Who made which API call, when and from where; an organization trail covers every account.
traps: Who changed it is CloudTrail; what the configuration was is Config.

Config.cue: Records resource configurations over time, checks them against rules and can remediate automatically.
traps: Config detects and remediates; it does not prevent changes (that is SCPs or IAM).

Systems Manager.cue: Operate fleets: Session Manager shells without SSH or bastions, Patch Manager, Run Command, Automation and Parameter Store.
traps: Shell access with no open port 22 and no bastion: Session Manager.

CloudFormation.cue: Infrastructure as code templates; StackSets deploy to many accounts and Regions.

Service Catalog.cue: Approved products, built on CloudFormation, that users can launch without broad permissions.

Trusted Advisor.cue: Checks across cost, security, fault tolerance, performance and service limits; the full set needs Business Support or higher.

Health Dashboard.cue: AWS events that affect your own resources, such as scheduled maintenance, with EventBridge integration.

X-Ray.cue: Distributed tracing to find latency and errors across microservices.

Managed Grafana.cue: Managed Grafana dashboards over CloudWatch, Prometheus and other data sources.

Service Quotas.cue: View and raise service limits, and alarm before you hit them.

Kinesis Data Streams.cue: Real-time streams in shards, read by many consumers in order, with replay within the retention period.
traps: Several consumers reading the same ordered stream in real time: Kinesis, not SQS.

Data Firehose.cue: Load streaming data into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch and others with no code, buffering and optional transformation.
traps: Firehose buffers, so it is near real time; there is no replay and no custom consumers.

Managed Service for Apache Flink.cue: Analyse streams in real time with SQL or Apache Flink apps.

MSK.cue: Managed Apache Kafka, for teams that already run Kafka.

Athena.cue: Serverless SQL straight on S3, paying per data scanned; partitions and columnar formats cut the cost.
traps: Convert to Parquet and partition to scan, and pay for, less data.

Glue.cue: Serverless ETL plus the Data Catalog that crawlers fill and Athena, EMR and Redshift Spectrum read.

EMR.cue: Managed Hadoop and Spark clusters for big data processing, often on Spot task nodes.
traps: Serverless ETL with no cluster to manage is Glue.

Lake Formation.cue: Build a data lake on S3 and grant fine-grained access down to columns and rows.
traps: Column- or row-level permissions on the data lake: Lake Formation, not bucket policies.

Redshift.cue: Columnar data warehouse for complex SQL analytics; Spectrum queries S3 without loading it.
traps: Ad hoc queries on S3 with no warehouse: Athena.

OpenSearch Service.cue: Full-text search and log analytics with dashboards.

QuickSight.cue: Serverless business intelligence dashboards with per-user pricing.

SageMaker.cue: Build, train and deploy your own machine learning models.
traps: If a ready-made AI service does the job, it is less effort than SageMaker.

Textract.cue: Extract text, forms and tables from scanned documents.
traps: Reading text from documents is Textract; understanding text is Comprehend.

Comprehend.cue: Natural language processing: sentiment, entities, key phrases and PII detection in text.
